synopsis: The manufacturer already offers proximity awareness that warns operators, while mining PDS evidence covers systems capable of stopping machines; the glossary characterizes underground PDS as the richest field evidence for that intervention [f9, f11658]. US regulation 30 CFR 75.1732 (2015) requires continuous-miner systems to warn audibly and visually and stop before contacting a miner, but specifies no numeric stop distance; no final rule was found for the separate 2015 proposal covering underground mobile machines [f2240, f2626, f7752]. Retrospective assessments judged 32 of 39 continuous-miner fatalities in 1984–2015 (82%) and 42 underground mobile-haulage fatalities in 1984–2014 potentially preventable by proximity systems, rather than demonstrating those reductions in deployment [f3095, f3098]. Nuisance interventions are the main documented reason systems were disabled: workers at seven mines reported unnecessary shutdowns ranging from once daily to 15 times during one coal cut, while production accounts range from a manufacturer's reported 5–10% loss to two operators reporting recovery to baseline [f116, f11659, f3029, f3030]. Integration readiness does not establish coverage or stopping adequacy: Epiroc requires all machines and persons to carry tags or sensors, Bell's coverage depends on the supplier, and NIOSH identified stopping-distance concerns when transferring slow-crawler systems to faster rubber-tired haulage [f1349, f1688, f1689, f6354]. Validation therefore remains equipment- and environment-specific, with NIOSH recording stop-zone differences averaging 1.4 m and reaching 3.6 m across nine field tests; intelligent PDS selectively disables hazardous motions, but published field-measured operator reaction-time distributions were not found [f5575, f10647, f5929, f6244, f11481].
